query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: High-temperature oxidation resistance in certain refractory HEAs is achieved by promoting the formation of a continuous CrTaO4-based oxide layer that limits cation and oxygen diffusion.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy containing significant fractions of Cr and Ta along with other refractory elements.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the Ta content in the alloy while keeping other elements constant to evaluate its influence on the formation and predominance of the CrTaO4 phase.
generation.conditions: Long-duration isothermal oxidation tests (100–200 hours) at high temperatures (1000–1100 °C) in an air environment.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous and adherent CrTaO4-based oxide layer that forms at the alloy surface and impedes diffusion.
generation.mechanism: In alloys with sufficient Ta, the element promotes the formation of a dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer. This layer effectively slows the outward diffusion of metal cations and the inward diffusion of oxygen. The kinetics of CrTaO4 formation, when optimized by appropriate Ta content, outweigh competing oxidation of other elements (e.g., formation of discontinuous Al2O3 or Cr2O3), thereby retarding overall oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with higher Ta content are predicted to exhibit a lower weight gain and a more uniform, protective oxide layer dominated by CrTaO4 compared to Ta-lean alloys under the same oxidation conditions.
generation.baseline: A comparable refractory HEA with reduced Ta content that forms mixed, non-uniform, or less adherent oxide layers.
generation.boundary: This mechanism operates effectively only in alloys where both Cr and Ta are present in adequate amounts; interference from other oxide-forming species at extreme conditions may alter the protective behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The detailed kinetics of CrTaO4 formation and its long-term stability in highly multicomponent systems, along with the specific Ta concentration required for optimal performance, need further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of refractory HEA samples with incremental Ta contents. Subject these samples to identical oxidation conditions (e.g., 1100 °C in air for 200 hours) and compare the characteristics of the oxide scales using phase identification and elemental mapping.
measurements: XRD and TEM analysis to identify the dominant oxide phases
EDS mapping for the distribution of Cr, Ta, and other elements within the oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing Ta content does not result in the formation of a predominantly CrTaO4-based oxide layer accompanied by improved oxidation resistance (lower mass gain and more uniform oxide), the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm2, which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. This work can also provide insights on how to further develop RHEA to w

In summary, isothermal oxidation at 1000 and 1100 °C was performed on a novel RHEA for up to 200 hours, such long-term oxidation test has not been reported before for this class of alloys. The weight gain behaviours during the tests could be affected by evolutions of external oxidation, internal oxidation, and nitridation. The multiple stages of weight gain behaviour at 1100 °C were never discussed in previous studies since most of them only presented the results of oxidation up to 48 hours,. We believe that CrTaO4-based protection layer and Si addition may be important for future development of RHEA against oxidation and nitridation. However, it is also possible that the growth of a protective Al2O3 or Cr2O3 layer was hindered by prominent CrTaO4-based oxide presence. In both cases, the nature of such CrTaO4-based oxide needs to be carefully examined in the future studies of RHEAs.
